say.text: Worked case first. A 50-year-old woman has a 2 cm invasive ductal carcinoma. Her armpit feels clear, and she wants to keep her breast.
Armpit: sentinel node biopsy stages a clinically node-negative axilla. Breast: conservation with clear margins plus whole-breast radiotherapy matches mastectomy survival in suitable early cancers.
Radiotherapy to the whole breast is mandatory after conservation, so keep all three steps in mind.
Same woman, same tumour. A classmate wrote a three-step plan, and one step is wrong.
Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 2: breast conservation rather than the radical operation
Step 1: clear levels I and II, sentinel node only if positive
Step 3: whole-breast radiotherapy once conservation is done
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A clinically node-negative armpit is staged by sentinel node biopsy, and clearance is reserved for node-positive disease.
Not right. Conservation sounds like the lesser operation beside a radical one, so it feels like the step to challenge.
Older keys named radical mastectomy the definitive operation. Conservation with radiotherapy matches mastectomy survival in suitable early cancers.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the radical operation was the old key's answer, not today's.

say.text: Not right. Radiotherapy can feel like an optional extra once the breast has been conserved, so this step looks like one to drop.
Whole-breast radiotherapy is mandatory after breast conservation, because the remaining breast tissue needs it.
Ask what the armpit step is for in a woman whose armpit is clear: to find out whether cancer has spread, or to clear the nodes anyway?
Step 1 is the wrong one. Clearing levels I and II before knowing the node status is the old order.
A clinically node-negative armpit is staged with sentinel node biopsy, and dissection follows only if the node is positive.
Now the reason. Why is clearing the armpit first the wrong order for this woman?

choices.label: It dissects an armpit that only needed staging
It is the classical first step, with biopsy only as a fallback
It risks lymphoedema, a real but secondary cost

say.text: Yes. Staging a node-negative armpit needs only the sentinel node, so a full clearance adds morbidity without answering a new question.
Not right. Clearance is the old key's first step, so it feels like the safe default.
Old keys cleared the armpit before knowing its status. For a clinically node-negative axilla, sentinel node biopsy is the standard staging.
Not right. Lymphoedema is a worry after clearance, so the step feels risky, and that makes it tempting.
Lymphoedema is a real complication of axillary dissection, but it is a cost of the step, not the reason the order is wrong.
The step is wrong because it dissects an armpit that only needed staging. Sentinel node biopsy stages a clinically node-negative armpit, and dissection follows only if the node is positive.
A woman has a 6 cm tumour in a moderate-sized breast. Chemotherapy shrinks it to 2 cm. A classmate's three-step plan has one wrong step.
Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 2: conservation is possible once it has shrunk to 2 cm
Step 1: a 6 cm tumour rules out conservation on size alone
Step 3: whole-breast radiotherapy after any conservation
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Size is judged against the breast and against cosmesis, so a 6 cm tumour is a relative problem, not an absolute bar to conservation.
Not right. Shrinkage to 2 cm looks like a loophole around a fixed size rule, so this step feels like the one to challenge.
Size is not an absolute bar. It is weighed against the breast and against cosmesis, which makes it a relative factor.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at the size rule: a fixed limit is not the test here.

say.text: Not right. Radiotherapy feels like the step to drop once the breast has been cut, so it looks like the weak point.
Whole-breast radiotherapy is mandatory after conservation, so this step is the standard one.
Ask what a 5 cm figure measures: the tumour alone, or the tumour against the breast it sits in.
Step 1 is the wrong one. A 6 cm tumour is a relative issue against breast size and cosmesis, not an absolute bar, so the step overstates the size rule.
A woman with operable cancer is not suitable for breast conservation.
Which operation should the plan name?

choices.label: Simple mastectomy, leaving the armpit for later
Halsted radical mastectomy, the definitive operation here
Modified radical mastectomy, preserving pectoralis major

say.text: Yes. Modified radical mastectomy removes the breast and the axillary nodes and keeps pectoralis major, so it is the alternative when conservation is unsuitable.
Not right. The definitive label from older keys makes the most extensive operation feel like the safe answer.
Halsted removed pectoralis major and minor along with all three axillary levels, and is now rarely done.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the most extensive operation is not today's default.

say.text: Not right. Deferring the armpit feels like a cautious shortcut when the breast is being removed anyway.
An operable cancer still needs the axilla dealt with at the same operation, so deferring it is not a safe plan.
The operation here is modified radical mastectomy. It removes the breast and the axillary nodes and keeps pectoralis major.
A classmate is counselling a woman after an axillary clearance. One of these three statements is wrong.
Which statement?

choices.label: The long thoracic nerve is the commonest nerve injured
The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed
Long thoracic injury causes winging of the scapula
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The long thoracic nerve causes the dramatic winging, but it is not the commonest injury. The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed.
Not right. Winging is the most dramatic deficit, so the nerve behind it feels like the most common one.
Frequency and drama are different questions. The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed, and its injury gives numbness of the medial arm.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate frequency from drama: they are different questions.

say.text: Not right. Winging is a vivid deficit, so a statement about it feels like the place to look for an error.
Long thoracic injury paralyses serratus anterior and makes the scapula wing. That statement is textbook.
Separate two questions: which nerve is injured most often, and which deficit is the most striking.
The wrong statement is the one calling the long thoracic nerve the commonest. It gives the striking winging, but the intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed.
